item.title: Supersonic passenger flight stalled for fifty years — the bottleneck was the engine, not aerodynamics
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.description: Concorde was banned not because the technology failed, but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban disappears. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and now it's being used first to generate power for data centers.
item.content:encoded:
Concorde was banned not because the technology failed, but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban disappears. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and now it's being used first to generate power for data centers.

The founder's own account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building his own engine and pivoting to data-center power generation, with specific numbers and regulatory detail, high information density.

5:12 Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
Boom's solution to the sonic boom is not to make the aircraft quiet, but to use the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back into the sky. Blake calls this boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff: the boom is still generated by the aircraft, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3, which is 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9 a.m. departure from New York and a 9:30 a.m. arrival in San Francisco still holds. Over the ocean no one is listening, so full speed is fine. Taken to its logical extreme: if there's no boom at all, there's nothing to argue about.

5:12 From executive order to congressional law, unanimous
The U.S. ban on supersonic flight over land, in place since 1973, ended on June 6 last year. But Blake knew an executive order could in theory be overturned by the next person, so he turned to pushing congressional legislation. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He put the significance plainly: supersonic isn't a partisan issue, which is how you get those vote counts. For a hardware company that needs to span multiple administrations and whose cycles are measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to law turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

6:12 Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, there was a public split with Rolls-Royce, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch themselves, and not just design it — even the hardest parts, like turbine blades, they make themselves. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing must be done together; if you want to reindustrialize America, you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed for Mach 1.7 high-temperature full-power long-duration operation, with the front fan removed and a generator attached at the back, is a power generation device.

8:13 The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
Boom's engine's first application isn't in the sky, it's on the ground. Remove the fan, swap in a generator at the back, put it in a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation, and because the engine core is designed to run at high temperature, it doesn't need water. Blake specifically points out that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, with a target of multiple gigawatts a year and adding more than 10 gigawatts to the grid over the next five years. The financial significance of this path: before the supersonic airliner gets its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell, and it's selling to the buyer with the least shortage of money right now.

10:14 Run on the ground first, then fly
Boom using the engine first for ground power generation has an engineering side effect: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for a huge number of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits many hard problems remain and success isn't guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over water, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally aviation engine validation relies on accumulating flight hours; Boom has moved validation to the ground and data-center scenarios, effectively using another market to pay the test costs for the aviation business.

10:38 Transatlantic round trip, breakeven fare $3,500
The numbers Blake gives: Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, actual ticket price probably higher, and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom aims to get all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he states clearly that ‘fast is more important than predictable’, can't give a definite date, and only promises to deliver at the earliest time physically possible, which outsiders read as around 2030. There's a trade-off worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it's unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

13:15 Data-center demand is so large it will be auctioned
Asked whether the data-center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and says his inbox has tens of gigawatts of demand. The first engine will fire up next month, and then they plan to auction off all the capacity. Asked whether he's talked to Elon, or whether it's for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this segment is that it gives a counterintuitive supply-demand signal: for a power product not yet in mass production, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing method has shifted from a quote to an auction.

16:19 Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
Blake recaps the speed of this regulatory push: Monday, break the sound barrier, tweet, Elon retweets, that night fly to Washington to start the legalization lobbying, and by landing he already had a White House invitation; Tuesday, into the West Wing; Thursday, the aircraft model went into the Oval Office, and it's still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he thinks is slow, but admits would be slower under a different administration. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how a technical milestone gets directly converted into political attention.

item.title: Why rebranding a charity is more dangerous than rebranding a company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.description: Mercy Corps became Prosper Global not because the strategy changed, but because the old name could no longer hold what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a new name can put staff more at risk.
item.content:encoded:
Mercy Corps became Prosper Global not because the strategy changed, but because the old name could no longer hold what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a new name can put staff more at risk.

Medium information density. The first half covers the disaster response and the rebranding logic; the second half, on the erosion of international humanitarian law and AI entering aid work, is where the value is.

4:21 The rename isn't a new strategy — the old name couldn't hold the business
Jada says an organisation's identity grows the way a person's does. The name Mercy Corps described the starting point of aid — rushing in to save people, handing out food, casting itself as the merciful giver. But what she now discusses with potential donors is cash assistance, seed insurance, identity management on blockchain, and the response she gets is flatly, "that has nothing to do with your name." The rename isn't a change of mission; mission and values are the source of continuity, the name is not. Prosper Global is meant to shorten the conversation and put the values up front: we believe every person has the capacity to prosper, not just to survive.

6:31 Renaming in a conflict zone puts safety on the line
Prosper Global operates in more than 30 countries, many of them remote sub-offices, often in conflict zones. Communities recognise the Mercy Corps colours and know who to look for. The rename means a phased rollout, one country at a time, with local people judging the timing and the context. Jada is blunt: they don't rate armed guards, they don't carry weapons, and their ability to work rests entirely on the trust of the communities they serve. So this is not an ordinary corporate logo swap — in the short term it may make frontline staff more vulnerable. The interesting part: 90% of staff live in the communities they serve, and many programme staff were the first to understand the rename — they don't want to be treated as "charity cases."

8:37 Syria is the clearest case for the rebranding logic
Driving from Aleppo to Damascus, Jada saw rubble the whole way. Syria has just come out of 14 years of civil war and is one of the few countries in the world where the population is returning rather than leaving, with millions going home at the same time. But many are still living in camps, and the communities they return to have no working water systems and destroyed houses. She tells the story of a woman named Ola: her husband was injured in the war, she hadn't worked before the war, and her community wasn't used to women doing certain things, so she was forced to take over the farming and start cultivating the land. Prosper Global helped her set up drip irrigation and repair the local water system, and along the way she learned to ride a motorcycle and brought another group of women along with her. Jada says Syria may be one of the world's rare pieces of good news, and it has been forgotten.

10:44 Oil in Hormuz decides whether African farmers plant at all
Prosper Global published a report called From Hormuz to Hunger, tracking how conflict in the Strait of Hormuz ripples into six fragile countries: Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar and Lebanon. The mechanism: these countries depend on Hormuz for basic fuel, and higher fuel prices hit fertiliser supply directly. When Jada was in Sudan, farmers had only a two-to-three-week window to get seeds in the ground, and fuel costs had already risen 60%. When farmers can't work out what to plant or which inputs they can afford, some of them decide to abandon the land. This isn't just a problem for today — it cripples next season's food supply too. At the same time, aid organisations are themselves paying higher oil prices, so the same money serves fewer people.

12:47 Ukraine's grain silos are being bombed on purpose
Prosper Global has just launched a grain storage project with the UN and the Ukrainian Red Cross. Jada says Ukraine's harvest this year is actually decent, but Russia is increasingly targeting civilian and economic infrastructure, especially grain silos and storage facilities, with drones. The logic is straightforward: even with a good harvest, if the silos and storage are destroyed, or the roads and ports are bombed so the grain can't move, that season's income is gone. This is a deliberate attack on that kind of infrastructure. What they do includes providing sleeved grain storage bags, helping farmers clear mines, and helping those who lost machinery rebuild or find alternatives. Ukraine was once the breadbasket for many countries, and it needs that grain to feed itself and its own economy.

14:47 Prevention is seven times cheaper than disaster response, and nobody wants to fund it
Jada says there is a tendency in the current relationship with the US government to fund only life-saving aid, which is in fact the least efficient way to do it. Her number: doing prevention, trying to stop a crisis from happening, is roughly seven times cheaper than intervening afterwards. She also says they were ready to rename as Prosper Global before the Trump administration came in, but held off because they needed to read the situation — the funding had already vanished and the whole sector was in a hard place. Instead they doubled down on helping Americans understand the nature of humanitarian need and what aid actually looks like today, correcting a lot of misinformation. She says the key to a leadership moment is intentionality: what are we letting go of, and what are we continuing to build on?

19:59 With USAID gone, the sector has to rebuild an architecture
Jada acknowledges they have to do more with less money, but stresses this isn't just about saving money — it's about rebuilding an architecture, in a sense. USAID's offices and missions around the world used to carry a huge amount of coordination and information-sharing, and now all of that is gone. So the question isn't just "can AI help" — it's that the sector's entire coordination layer has been pulled out. She says AI can't physically deliver supplies for you, and it has limits in knowledge, but it's useful at the programme level: accessing best practices, pinpointing more precisely what a community needs, anticipating certain needs. They haven't found the magic solution yet, but they're talking to AI companies, hoping to build something together that genuinely changes humanitarian aid.

23:02 International humanitarian law is eroding, starting with Ukraine
Jada says the checks on international humanitarian law are being tested and violated, and that this is part of a broader trend. She thinks the first case seen as a deliberate pattern was Russia's invasion of Ukraine — attacks on ports, bridges and other civilian infrastructure traditionally treated as untouchable followed quickly. Then the pattern spread to the way the war in Sudan is being fought, and they believe violations of international law are also occurring in Gaza. She notes it took the deaths and destruction of millions after World War II to bring these rules into being: no collective punishment, people must be able to go to school and have a hospital network, civilians shouldn't pay the price. Now those rules are being violated everywhere. She says even the phrase "international humanitarian law" sounds like Greek to a lot of people.

item.title: In the AI Era, the Most Valuable Thing Isn't Intelligence — It's the Audit Trail
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.description: Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.
item.content:encoded:
Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.

Worth hearing for vertical AI founders, investment banking/PE practitioners, and enterprise software investors. The first half's product history is middling in information density; the pricing, audit, and sales mechanics in the back half are worth more.

2:03 Model companies are refineries; vertical companies are chemical plants
Gabe reasons from Dario's line: if a whole data center full of geniuses showed up tomorrow at the door of Goldman, Millennium, Citadel, those institutions would still take a long time to figure out how to change how they work and how to wire it into their systems. So he thinks the biggest challenge for every great investor over the next five years isn't getting access to intelligence, it's wiring AI into the investment lifecycle. It also explains why he isn't worried about Anthropic and OpenAI: finance is a collection of niches with wildly different data, definitions, and regulatory requirements, and for Anthropic to stop and pick up this coin would be pulling over on the road from $100 billion in revenue to $1 trillion.

4:04 Applied AI companies have a first-mover disadvantage
Gabe says the companies that did applied AI early were actually at a disadvantage: you think you know where the world is going, you build the product for that end state, but the models aren't there yet, and users try it and just say ‘this is garbage.’ Rogo went through that phase itself. His judgment is that if your read on the end state is right and you keep building toward it, the moment the models catch up is the magic moment. He ties Rogo's product eras directly to model eras: 01 Pro was the first version reliable enough to at least serve as a search tool; by Opus 4.5, and from late 2025 into early 2026, the models can basically do anything a junior investment or banking professional does, provided you give the right instructions and context.

6:06 The MD annotating on an iPad is the real last mile
Gabe gives an example as concrete as it gets: the typical workflow for an investment banking MD is to email deck comments to an analyst, and Rogo lets that MD email the comments to an AI analyst instead, getting a revised draft back in 20 minutes instead of two days, while automatically notifying the junior analysts on the deal and showing a full audit trail of every small change. He points out the key: this finance professional hasn't logged into a computer in ten years, but he has an iPad, and he knows how to annotate on an iPad. That kind of product detail for a specific end user can only come from someone with a spidey sense for the job.

16:57 The harness matters more than the model itself
Gabe compares Claude Code and Claude Cowork against ChatGPT: the models are actually similar, but Claude's harness and presentation are so much better that they let the model exercise more long-horizon capability, and usage and expansion took off. He extends the analogy to the brain: humans have high agency not just because of raw memory, IQ, and knowledge, but because there are a bunch of microservices in the head — how knowledge is stored, how it's retrieved, how it's triggered, and emotion is one way of triggering a microservice. A great investor's judgment comes from seeing something in the market that triggers the memory of some event, producing a creative decision. Those microservices are what vertical companies have to build.

23:43 Skip seat-based pricing and go straight to outcome-based
Rogo today is classic enterprise software: priced per seat, because buyers are used to comparing it to Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, PitchBook, and every deal signed needs an AE plus a solutions architect to shake hands and explain the integration. Gabe says Anthropic can sell to them easily, with spend rising exponentially and no human involvement, because it's a token-consumption model; but many industries can't ride the token-consumption wave, and Rogo is one of them, so it has to build its GTM machine at five times the speed. His pricing judgment is that every enterprise goes through two pricing revolutions: first to usage-based, then to outcome-based. He'd rather skip tokens and usage entirely and ask the customer directly: how much do you pay me per good investment idea? Per quarterly LP report? Per investment banking CIM?

31:19 Auditability matters more than accuracy
Gabe says accuracy is of course still super important, but auditability matters more than accuracy, and the two get conflated all the time. The logic: if the answer is wrong and you don't know how to check it or see where it came from, then whether it's accurate or not you can't use it, because you don't trust it. Conversely, if it's right most of the time and even when it's wrong you can clearly see the assumptions and the data sources, it's still actionable and still saves time. As tools move from copilot to autopilot — not just retrieving information but having agency, actually making investment decisions or sending emails — you have to be able to look back at why it decided that way, because you need to debug it, just as when an individual investor makes a bad decision you check whether the data input was wrong or someone lied to him. In regulated capital markets, if you can't explain the basis for a decision, you simply don't get through.

34:48 The company brain is called Shrek, and every conversation is recorded
Every conversation inside Rogo is recorded, and new hires are told on day one ‘you are always being recorded,’ and that content is filtered into the company brain, named Shrek because the engineers thought that was funny. There's a dashboard showing the ‘swamp’ of what everyone is working on, connected to the company's various systems, with a very clear view of company goals, values, what has to be delivered to customers, and the north star metric, so it can shape every answer and deliverable. It's both passive and active: you can go in and ask ‘how do I pitch the value proposition and savings of model routing to a large institution,’ and it pulls the information out; it also proactively reminds you, ‘Patrick, I see you're meeting this private credit firm on Thursday, here's what you should know, the use cases that will resonate, and the ROI metrics companies you've worked with before want to hear.’ Gabe says this is the core problem of enablement: suck information in, and give it out when people need it.

42:18 What it's like to be turned down by 40 investors in a row
Gabe says the hardest low point was the A round: at that point there were no star investors on the cap table, David Tisch introduced him to 40 investors, he met Sequoia, Kleiner, Benchmark and others, and all 40 passed. And not the send-a-deck-no-interest kind — it was ‘interesting, meet Gabe,’ ‘like Gabe, chat for an hour,’ ‘come to IC,’ ‘grab a meal,’ ‘come back over the weekend’ — and then ‘we've decided not to invest.’ He says that phase had nothing to do with anything except you, like being dumped by 40 girlfriends, each time you fell in love and each time they said it wasn't for you. In the end Thrive didn't invest either; Keith Rabois came about a month after everyone had passed, and Gabe asked Keith back: if this isn't a contrarian bet, why did all your friends say it was a bad idea and not believe in me? He sums up three reasons investors didn't invest: they underestimated the finance TAM, the product really was bad at the time, and there weren't enough data points to believe he could chew glass and ship the next version.

item.title: The Rocky Statue Is Not Art, Yet It Became a Landmark Philadelphia Can't Tear Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.description: A bronze made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — and in the end what saved it wasn't artistic merit but that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.
item.content:encoded:
A bronze made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — and in the end what saved it wasn't artistic merit but that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.

Thirty minutes that carries one complete narrative line: class, artistic authority, race and monument politics, dense with detail and almost no filler.

4:09 Bronze instead of foam is what decided its fate
In Rocky III there's a scene: a fictional mayor stands on the museum steps and dedicates a statue to Philadelphia. The production could have had the art department build a prop out of painted plastic and foam and toss it in a dumpster after shooting. Stallone didn't do that — he paid $53,000 to have the artist A. Thomas Schaumburg cast the statue in bronze. Laura Holzman says that choice was crucial: the material wasn't something you throw away after filming, it was an art material. Stallone went to high school in Philadelphia, called Rocky a "euphemism" for the city, and then offered to donate the 1,800-pound statue to Philadelphia to stand permanently at the top of the steps. It's precisely because it was bronze and not foam that the next fifty years of fighting were even possible.

10:25 The root of the opposition was Philadelphia wanting to be Athens
The museum leadership opposed it hardest, and their reasons were far bigger than aesthetics. Philadelphia's glory days had long faded by the early 20th century, and by the 1976 Bicentennial it was the city that could never shake its bad luck: crumbling infrastructure, corrupt local politics. In the 1980s the arts crowd wanted to remake Philadelphia as a cultural metropolis and restore the title a famous architect had given it — "the Athens of the Western world." They had bet heavily on the city's most important museum, and they didn't see how a nine-foot-tall, sharply abdominals boxing could help Philadelphia toward that dream. Art commission chairman F. Eugene Dixon Jr. wrote to colleagues that the statue standing temporarily on the steps was fine, but permanently in the courtyard, "I hope you're joking." In the winter of 1980 the commission voted 6 to 2 against permanent placement, and the remaining two votes were to ban it from the steps outright.

12:34 Thousands of signatures lose to eight people with votes
What brought the statue back to Philadelphia from Los Angeles was a grassroots campaign. Local truck driver Art Gorman was one of its biggest champions — Mark Bowden describes him as a straight-talking Philadelphia guy from a blue-collar neighborhood, thinking: who are these self-appointed tastemakers to tell us what we can see on the steps of the art museum. At the end of 1980 he drafted a petition, all in capital letters, knocked on doors for thousands of signatures, and drew a pile of media coverage. The show says it plainly: the story got told as blue-collar Philadelphia versus elite high-culture Philadelphia, a "slobs versus snobs" narrative. But the petition couldn't change the commission's basic position — the snobs were still the ones voting.

13:34 The prop crew bolted the statue into the ground with steel bars
Rocky III opened in May 1982, and the art commission only allowed the statue back on the steps for the premiere; once it was over, it had to go. But the production company simply left it there, the city wouldn't pay to move it, and it fell to the museum to deal with. Months later the movers finally came and found an obstacle: the statue was bolted to the sidewalk with steel bars driven several feet into the ground — "as if the filmmakers intended it to stay there forever." In the end the statue was pried loose and hauled five miles away to the Spectrum arena in South Philadelphia, where it stood with other athletes' statues. Most people thought the fight was over, but Stallone spent the next twenty-five years repeatedly asking for it to return to the museum, and every time he got the same answer: no.

15:35 One phone call did more than twenty years of aesthetic debate
In 2006 things moved: the mayor was pushing a batch of public-space renovation projects, Stallone was about to release his first Rocky film in 16 years, and the statue was sitting in a warehouse because the city was building a new sports complex. Stallone's friend Jimmy Binns — who appeared in the sequels and is a lawyer with real clout in Philadelphia — called the mayor and asked whether he'd help get the statue back to the museum. Binns recounted the conversation: he asked the mayor, do those museum trustees invite you to their homes for cocktails on Sundays? The mayor laughed and said no. Binns said, then to hell with them. The mayor said, alright, to hell with them. With the mayor behind it, even the Philadelphia Museum of Art started to give ground, and the compromise worked out was: the statue returns to the museum permanently, but not at the top of the steps — off to one side at the bottom. The only remaining obstacle was the art commission, which held the final vote.

19:46 By 2006 the debate was no longer about art
In May 2006 the commission announced it might move the statue, setting off a new round of public discussion. City official Harris Baum argued against it on local NPR's call-in show, on the grounds that the Parkway was to be developed into a cultural district like Paris's, "but that is not a work of art." The response he got was completely different from the 1980s: listeners didn't want to talk about art. Judy said the statue was an image of the blue-collar spirit; Jack, calling from Lansdale, said ideally he'd want it at the top of the steps, but a bunch of pretentious old guys in wigs would never let that happen, and he called Baum a snob and an insult to the people. Baum was fighting the battle of twenty years earlier. On September 6, 2006, the art commission voted 6 to 2 in favor, and the minutes read: the majority believed the statue's iconic symbolic meaning had earned it a place in the city's identity. Less than a week later the statue was unveiled, fitted with nighttime lighting, and raised onto a brand-new granite pedestal.

26:14 The real champion's steps are called the Rocky steps
The 2015 Charleston church shooting, in which nine people were killed, set off a national reckoning with racist symbols, and the wind reached Philadelphia: the Columbus statue and the statue of former mayor Frank Rizzo — known for violent policing and racist demagogy — became targets. When Monument Lab asked Philadelphians what kind of monuments they wanted to build, some began questioning whether Rocky was appropriate: Philadelphia has a real boxing history, and those boxers were mostly Black, including heavyweight champion Joe Frazier, who beat Muhammad Ali in a fight watched by more than 300 million people. The show points out that the two most famous things in the first Rocky training montage — running up the museum steps and punching raw meat — actually came from Frazier's real training routine. Frazier got a statue in 2015, but many Philadelphians feel the twelve-foot bronze falls far short of a real champion: "His image isn't on the tour buses, and the steps he ran up are called the Rocky steps."

28:21 In the reckoning over monuments, Rocky became the city's emotional container
After George Floyd was killed in 2020, Philadelphia's largest Black Lives Matter demonstrations set out from the art museum steps every day, with thousands of protesters gathering right beside the Rocky statue. By then it was already a monument, and by rights it should have faced the same scrutiny — a statue put up for a fictional white movie character, taking the place of a real Black champion, its days should have been numbered. But no one tore it down; instead they folded it in: someone hung a sign on it reading "no justice, no peace," early in the pandemic it wore a mask, later a Ukrainian flag, and when the Eagles' Brandon Graham retired, his cleats were hung on it. Paul Farber saw the most contradictory scene: a Black family taking a photo all raising Black Power fists, and three or four people later, a group of white men in their early twenties raising white power gestures — the two things happening almost simultaneously without conflict.

item.title: Vitamin K injection refusal rates have doubled, and infant brain bleeds are preventable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.description: Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular shot drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates rose from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.
item.content:encoded:
Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular shot drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates rose from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.

High information density: it covers both the clinical mechanism of newborn bleeding and the discovery of vitamin K, plus how a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust. The back half, on who refuses and why communication fails, is the most valuable part.

20:34 Every newborn is born deficient in vitamin K
Vitamin K does not cross the placenta effectively, so even if the mother supplements during pregnancy, the newborn's vitamin K-dependent clotting factors do not rise appreciably. Add an immature gut microbiome, very little self-synthesised K2, and breast milk averaging only about 2.5 micrograms per litre, and a exclusively breastfed infant gets less than 1 microgram a day for the first six months. The result is that every newborn is at high risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. This is not an outlier phenomenon; it is the physiological norm.

22:35 Late bleeding often comes with no warning, straight to brain haemorrhage
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns comes in three types: early, within 24 hours of birth; classic, within the first week; and late, from one week to six months. Late is the most dangerous: about 60% of cases are intracranial haemorrhage, and there is often no warning bleed beforehand, just sudden brain haemorrhage, seizures or unresponsiveness. Mortality ranges from 50% to 60% depending on era and country, with modern figures around 20%. That is why the value of a single preventive shot cannot be measured by ‘the bleeding probability is low’.

25:46 A single intramuscular shot pushes the risk to near zero
Since 2003 in the US, and in the vast majority of medical societies and public health agencies worldwide, a single intramuscular vitamin K injection at birth has been recommended. It provides a stable supply through the first few months, cutting late bleeding risk from 4 to 7 cases per 100,000 live births (some countries report as high as 80) to about 0.4. Infants who receive no prophylaxis have 81 times the risk of late bleeding compared with those who do. Oral regimens also significantly reduce risk, but require multiple doses, are affected by absorption and vomiting, and are less effective than injection; the US has no regulator-approved oral formulation.

44:27 How a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust
In the postwar research climate, informed consent and patient protections had not yet entered the picture, and the logic was ‘vitamin is harmless and possibly beneficial, so give it to all premature infants’. In the mid-1950s Britain gave some premature infants up to 60 milligrams of synthetic vitamin K, after which jaundice, haemolysis and kernicterus rose, and several infants died. The formulation was withdrawn and the dose dropped back to 1 milligram, but confidence had been shaken: of more than 16,000 infants born in Britain in a single week in 1970, only 20% received vitamin K. This history shows that the aftershocks of a single overdose incident can last for decades.

46:31 The 1990s leukaemia scare still has not cleared
In the early 1990s two British studies linked intramuscular vitamin K to later leukaemia risk, and the reaction was swift and strong: some countries switched to recommending oral dosing and reserved injections for the highest-risk infants, and British injection rates fell from 58% in 1988 to 38% in 1993. But both studies had small samples and insufficient control variables, and a large body of subsequent research and a WHO working group found no association, with IARC also concluding there was no evidence of carcinogenicity. The problem is that bad news travels fast and good news does not, just like MMR and autism: once doubt is planted, the world never quite recovers.

49:35 Refusal rates have doubled, and the 81-fold risk is badly underestimated
US refusal rates nearly doubled from 2017 to 2024, rising from 3% to 5.8%, with some hospitals reporting higher. Infants whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a figure that is badly underestimated because the bleeding itself remains rare and communication is inadequate. Research shows most parents, whether they accept or refuse, know vitamin K is related to bleeding, but do not know that this bleeding can cause severe brain injury and a mortality risk above 20%. The information is present, but it is not being effectively conveyed.

50:36 Refusals fall into three categories, and the birth attendant matters enormously
Reasons for refusal fall roughly into three categories: distrust of medicine, pursuit of ‘natural birth’, and preference for alternative medical lifestyles. Some believe that if infants needed more vitamin K, evolution or God would have provided it; some read the recommendation to supplement vitamin K as ‘you are not fit to be a mother’. Research also finds refusers are more likely to be white, college-educated, over 30, and planning a home or birth-centre delivery. The birth attendant's stance is critical: in a New Zealand survey, 100% of doctors thought all infants should receive vitamin K, while only 55% of midwives did, and 26% of those would not give it to their own children; in Canada, infants delivered by midwives were 8 times more likely to have vitamin K refused than those delivered by doctors.

55:46 Doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time
Some parents who lost a child or whose child suffered brain injury because vitamin K was not given are doing something very brave: speaking publicly to say ‘I made this decision, this is the consequence, do not follow me’. At the same time, doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time in their careers, and they are raising the alarm in their communities. Some researchers and doctors are pushing to establish a national US registry of vitamin K refusals and administrations, because vitamin K deficiency bleeding is not a notifiable disease and cases are likely undercounted. In a post-pandemic era when expertise is treated as a dirty word, these preventable injuries and deaths will keep increasing.

item.title: Making a Child Perform Isn't Connection, It's Depletion
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.description: Connection isn't getting your child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.
item.content:encoded:
Connection isn't getting your child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.

This episode isn't dense — it's a single-topic parenting podcast. But if you're dealing with relatives pushing your child to perform, or you want to understand what "connection" actually means, it's worth a listen.

1:04 Making a child perform is fast-food connection
A mother writes in that her 17-month-old son can identify shapes and colors, speak in sentences, and name dinosaurs, but his grandmother keeps making him "perform" — repeating what he's learned, clapping — and when he won't cooperate she grabs his arm and does it for him, and recently even kicked him in the butt. Janet says this isn't an isolated case: we often think connecting with infants and toddlers means getting them to react to us, to imitate us. But this is "fast-food connection." The child may smile because he's getting attention, but no one is truly seen.

4:08 We're performing too
Connection goes both ways: we don't just make children perform, we're often performing ourselves rather than being ourselves. In her forthcoming book Baby Person, Janet writes that she used to dance, make funny faces, and try every trick to get a reaction out of babies in order to bond with them. These surface methods left her exhausted, and the payoff was tiny and fleeting — "I made her laugh" is just a moment. She says this isn't deep connection; it's all surface.

6:14 Performance connection teaches children to be insincere
Janet lists five reasons connection shouldn't be a performance: one, it isn't real connection; two, it teaches children to be insincere — everything we do with children teaches them something, and this teaches that "connection requires performing rather than being yourself"; three, it wastes energy and effort, and parents can't afford it; four, it doesn't satisfy, and doesn't move the relationship toward trust; five, it subtly belittles the child — why should a child have to perform to hold our attention and interest?

8:19 Charismatic people are charismatic because they're paying attention to you
Janet quotes something she's always remembered: certain people are charismatic to us not because of how they perform or what they put out, but because they're genuinely interested in us and paying attention to us. Children need this especially, because it's harder for them to express themselves proactively and they don't know what to say to connect. They need us to tune in to their subtleties: what they're interested in, what their expressions are saying, who they are.

9:19 Even a parenting expert couldn't connect with her grandchild
Janet read a book by a well-known psychologist treated as a parenting expert, in which the author, now a grandparent, said she simply couldn't connect with a toddler grandchild and felt the child had no chemistry with her. Janet's immediate judgment: this grandparent was trying too hard — wanting to initiate games, wanting the child to cooperate, was "working it" rather than connecting. Her method works for every child from infancy on: observe, listen, receive, pay attention.

10:21 Comment on what you see instead of pretending to be interested
The concrete approach: treat the child as a person with depth, talent, interests, and a real point of view worth knowing. Then comment on what you see — "You're looking over there, did you hear a dog?" "You seem really interested in those blocks, I see you lining them up." Not pretending to be interested, but actually becoming interested. Children can tell the difference between "good job" and "wow, that took a while, I saw you thinking about which one goes on top, and the round one rolled down."

12:31 Children can put a grandparent's behavior in context
How do you let go of the fear that "this is bad for the child"? Janet says children are more aware than we think. They know "this is my grandparent, this isn't how my parents are with me, this is just how this person is." So it won't affect how they feel about themselves. Parents have enormous influence, but grandparents are different — even with frequent contact, children can put it in the context of "my relationship with that person."

14:34 Narrate instead of correcting
Janet advises this mother not to try to teach her mother or correct her, but to connect, reflect, and trust them to handle the relationship themselves. Concretely: if her son does what the grandmother asks, let it go; if he doesn't and the grandmother kicks him, don't say to the grandmother "you shouldn't do that," but say to her son "Grandma really likes it when you do what she asks, she's really into this" — without sarcasm, just stating what's happening. This is called sportscasting, and it helps both the child and the grandmother understand what's going on.

item.title: The Pentagon doesn't lack models — it lacks the chain that puts intelligence on the president's desk
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.description: The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft — it was procurement reform, the intelligence analysis agencies, and the chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it. APIs alone are not enough.
item.content:encoded:
The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft — it was procurement reform, the intelligence analysis agencies, and the chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it. APIs alone are not enough.

The first half uses the U-2 analogy to lay out clearly where the government's AI integration bottleneck is; the second half's judgments on procurement incentives, token economics and cybersecurity are worth more, but overall it's a loose interview chat with medium information density.

2:02 The U-2's miracle wasn't the plane, it was the procurement and analysis chain
Garrett says the U-2 story is usually told as a technology breakthrough, but what really mattered was three things: procurement reform that let government and industry work together that way, intelligence analysis being institutionalized (NPIC, which later became NGA), and getting judgment in front of the president and other decision-makers. That, he says, is the ‘miraculous’ part of the story. Today's AI problem is the exact inverse: the technology comes from the commercial world, moves too fast, and has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it into systems, workflows and decision processes — so ‘APIs alone are not enough’.

9:06 AI is advancing fastest in warfighting, slowest in business systems
Garrett says the Pentagon and other departments have made visible progress in warfighting spaces like CJADC2: using AI to build situational awareness across the battlefield, identify targets, and push intelligence quickly to decision-makers at the front. But core business systems — logistics, personnel, finance — have seen the least progress. His personal view is that we should stop dividing systems into ‘mission systems’ and ‘business systems’, because supporting the front line requires clean, well-organized data usable at operational tempo, and those business systems were never built for operational tempo.

10:06 One policy rule blocks the data of twenty thousand logistics troops
He gives a concrete example: some business systems' rules say status only needs to be updated once a week. That's policy — someone wrote it down. But decision-makers now want that data daily, which means going to roughly ten or twenty thousand Army supply sergeants and saying ‘you have to enter it daily, not weekly’. That's ‘a big boat to turn around’, and it has to come with clear value. Worse, the systems the government gave them are already bad to use — making it hard to enter data while demanding a big drop in data latency.

14:10 Government has no market competition as a forcing function
The host points out that companies that don't do AI get eliminated, but the Air Force or the national security apparatus won't be ‘competed out’ — that kind of forcing function comes once or twice a century. Garrett agrees, but says we underestimate our ability to manufacture mechanisms ourselves. He argues for using personnel policy and leadership as carrot and stick: reward people who take risks and take strange career paths, and let those who move too slowly face career stagnation or removal. He says it sounds ‘crude’, but that's the mechanism you have to follow.

19:18 Second-mover advantage: watch others burn money and hit the pits first
Garrett says this time it's the reverse of the U-2: the technology happens in the commercial sector first and then enters government, so government has second-mover advantage and can see what's working. He cites the lesson of token economics: do you open it up like Uber and let everyone burn tokens without limit, blowing the budget in a quarter, or do you first understand token economics and then deploy to employees? Also, as the federal government, if it gets this right it can act as a supersized buyer and negotiate volume pricing.

23:20 To put GPUs at the edge, first clear the policy on who signs and who's liable
Garrett says if you put these tools in soldiers' hands, you'll be shocked at how innovative and clever they are at using them for their actual jobs — which may mean pushing compute to the edge, putting GPUs in service members' hands. But the obstacle is policy: a logistics officer signs for $500,000 worth of chips, and who's responsible if a chip breaks? He says you have to clear the policy and just say ‘we own this risk’, and if it means some GPUs get broken and money is lost, that's worth it, because capability reaches the edge.

29:26 Intelligence analysis is more tractable than modeling decisions
Garrett thinks using AI to model strategic decisions is very hard, because it needs good data, and the decision process is deliberately opaque — you can't get all the private notes, emails and situation-room audio and video. But intelligence analysis is a more tractable project: the intelligence process is structured and rigorous, agencies have their own SOPs and training, there are decades of data, and there are signals of quality high and low that you can build benchmarks against. Still, it's only one input to decisions — historically many decision-makers looked at the same intelligence and made completely different decisions.

38:36 Bill by the hour and people will report more hours
Garrett says the government buys a great deal on hourly rates by person and seniority, and this time and materials structure has a status quo bias. The logic is plain: if the incentive is for companies to report more hours, and there's no hard delivery requirement when the hours run out, they will report more hours. He says there have been signs of change over the past 12 to 18 months, but looking at public spending data, there's no large-scale shift — most spending is still time and materials. He also mentions that top companies spend 10% of their budget on tokens, while the US government is far below that level.

item.title: Procrastination isn't a willpower problem: next time you'll fail with the same plan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.description: Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it hurts you, and about one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need a different fix — but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan, and nothing about the outcome changes.
item.content:encoded:
Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it hurts you, and about one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need a different fix — but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan, and nothing about the outcome changes.

It breaks procrastination into types you can actually treat and hands you a concrete toolbox instead of another "just be disciplined" pep talk. Medium-high information density.

1:16 The definition of procrastination has reluctance baked into it
Itamar's definition is: we delay something even though we don't intend to delay it, and we know it's bad for us. So "I deliberately decided to do it later and I feel fine about that" is not procrastination. The grey zone is: what if you think delaying is good for you but it's actually harmful? His test is "could you have expected this to be better for you." About 20% of adults procrastinate chronically; among students it's 50%. He stresses that procrastination doesn't only happen to people who don't care — people high in conscientiousness, genuinely productive, who truly want to make an impact, procrastinate too.

3:27 Procrastination is several types, not one thing
Treating procrastination as a single phenomenon makes two mistakes at once: you fail to see that it happens to people other than students, and you can't deal with it in practice. A student who procrastinates from distraction, an executive who procrastinates from burnout and an artist who procrastinates from perfectionism have different drivers and need different solutions. In his book Itamar distinguishes the anxious type, the type pulled away by external temptations, the burnout type, and a category he calls zigzaggers — closer to ADHD and impulsivity, switching back and forth between internal rather than external distractions.

5:00 Anxiety cuts both ways: fear of the task vs. fear of the consequences
The mechanism by which anxiety causes procrastination is: doing this hurts, the brain says I don't want to hurt, so you put it off. But anxiety also has an adaptive side — if what you're anxious about isn't the task itself but the consequences of not finishing it, a little anxiety pushes you to act. The key variables are intensity and self-efficacy: a little anxiety may motivate you, a lot of anxiety paralyzes you no matter what it's aimed at; and if you also believe you're incapable of finishing, anxiety turns into paralysis more easily. Itamar adds one caveat: even when anxiety does push you, it's a dangerous source of motivation, because it brings stress and a worse experience along with it.

9:25 The biggest mistake is believing you'll try harder next time
Itamar says the biggest mistake people make when tackling procrastination is falling into the self-control fallacy: believing that next time, if you just try harder and summon more willpower, you'll pull it off. The absurdity is that we watch it fail over and over, and over and over we believe again. The reasons include the bias blind spot (failing to recognize your own biases) and the empathy gap (predicting, in a calm state, what you'll do in a hot emotional state). The real harm of this belief is that it offers a superficially minimal silver bullet, which stops you from looking for what actually works. Spencer's addition: change nothing, and nothing changes.

12:45 Design for your future self as if they were someone else
Spencer's approach: don't assume that the you of two weeks from now will get it done on willpower — instead ask "what would help a person very much like me get this done in two weeks" — set reminders, make social commitments, add rewards. Itamar says this is exactly an illustration of his core claim: procrastination isn't a time management problem, and even excellent time management can fail; what you should be doing is distance management. Addressing yourself in the second or third person, or using your name instead of "I", or asking "what advice would I give a friend", all create psychological distance and help you enter wise reasoning, seeing through the situation and around your biases.

16:13 Anxious type: decatastrophize, or do it anxious
For the anxious procrastinator, Itamar's first choice is to decatastrophize: catastrophizing means overestimating both the probability that something bad happens and the harm it does to you. For example, "there's a typo in my proposal, so the agent will blacklist me, and will tell everyone else to blacklist me too." The move is to ask: how likely is this really? If it happened, how bad would it be? If it happened, how would I carry on? Spencer offers an almost opposite strategy: notice that this task makes me anxious, sit inside that feeling, feel it, and then do it anyway — he calls it metacognitive awareness. Itamar files it under the umbrella of mindfulness and self-compassion.

21:39 Procrastination is short-term emotional repair, and it reinforces itself
Spencer points out that anxiety generates anxiety: the moment you say "I'm not doing this now", the anxiety usually drops immediately, so you're learning that procrastination makes you feel better, forming a reinforcement loop. Doing the opposite unwinds it — doing it while anxious functions like an exposure. Itamar says procrastination here is a defense mechanism: because you feel pressure or anxiety about something you should do, you push it away to avoid the painful emotion. It makes you feel better short term and worse long term, because you haven't solved the problem — you've only arranged to face it again and again later, or to face worse consequences.

26:39 The burnout fix is to do less
Itamar admits this is the last thing burned-out people want to hear: if you're burned out because you're doing too much, or doing things that drain you, you probably need to do less and take more deliberate care of yourself — concretely, deciding more deliberately what to do and, more importantly, what not to do. He describes a loop: you're used to performing well, burnout makes your performance drop, so you work harder, so you burn out more, and it gets worse and worse. He calls this "borrowing health and productivity from your future self." He also notes that burnout doesn't come only from hours: reasonable hours spent on high-pressure, meaningless or otherwise draining tasks will burn you out just the same.

item.title: The cost of RLHF is mode dropping, not alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.description: RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative in order to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.
item.content:encoded:
RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative in order to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.

High information density: Diogo goes deep on the trade-offs between RLHF, RLVR and RLCD, suited to anyone who needs to form a judgment on model training routes.

6:03 The cost of RLHF is mode dropping
Diogo thinks nobody pays attention to RLHF's downsides, especially mode dropping. The mechanism: to generate very long strings without making a mistake, the model has to be extremely conservative, because errors are visible at a glance while things that look correct but are subtly wrong are very hard to spot; this calibration is "total poison" for the probability distribution over strings. He uses this to explain why Yann LeCun's chart showing that LLMs necessarily make errors as sequences get longer is mathematically obvious but empirically false — when you cover the distribution you don't get over-penalized by outliers; it's mode drop that throws away the minority classes.

11:12 Refusing to answer is a type error, not a safety problem
Diogo distinguishes safety alignment from capability alignment: the latter is "doing what the user wants," the former is "following someone else's instructions," as with OpenAI and Anthropic. He thinks safety alignment is reasonable for products like ChatGPT and Claude, but in an API it is "nuts," "completely unacceptable" — if a dependency is running in the background, having your software randomly crash because a user sent one weird message is insanity. He opposes putting restrictions at the technical layer on the grounds that every overfit fractures intelligence a little more, and today's models are already fractured enough.

18:15 Public benchmarks are a substitute for trust
Diogo says he is extremely anti-public benchmarks because they are extremely gameable: in the early days every lab had a team dedicated to collecting data like MMLU to pump up scores, which is essentially "benchmarking with extra steps." He admits intelligence has a je ne sais quoi (good model smell), so people need benchmarks to build trust, but in the long run you can only rely on vibes and trust, until you put the model into a concrete workflow and evaluate it there. He also says that if they wanted to make Jev dumb, they could have shipped it a year and a half ago.

27:34 RLCD is a new North Star, not a new algorithm
Diogo says the term RLHF has been conflated: the original work was Paul Christiano teaching a robot to do a backflip, then it was learning to summarize, and only later did it become instruction following. What he actually calls RLHF is "instruction following as the North Star," with nothing to do with the PPO algorithm — just as DPO and its descendants don't use that paper's algorithm and still count as RLHF. RLCD is the same: a new task direction, programs in the loop, taking the human out of the loop.

40:38 Reliability is a catchall; the North Star is robustness
Diogo defines reliability as a catchall: if AI can't automate something, in the end it's always some kind of reliability problem — it might be type safety, it might be determinism, or it might just be that the model is too jagged. He explicitly rejects determinism (same input, same output) as the North Star, holding that it is only slightly valuable for unit tests; what really matters is robustness — similar inputs getting similar outputs. The test is to stuff nonces like UUIDs into the prompt and see whether semantically identical questions get similar answers. He says that when people get burned by AI decisions, that's the layer where it happens.

1:17:12 Reliability is more underrated than speed and cost
Diogo thinks the industry has its attention in the wrong place: "people focus too much on speed and cost and not enough on reliability." His judgment is that reliability is what makes people delighted and what makes them dare to trust. He ties this to TFP growth — he expects TFP growth above 3% within five years, and says that is the mark of an economic revolution, and also what the OpenAI charter originally meant to express. He estimates that all current models are still roughly at zero, maybe not even 1%, on valuable work in the world economy.

1:44:10 The optimal dose of RLVR is zero
Diogo says outright that for a model of TypeSafe's shape, the optimal amount of RLVR is zero. His argument is not "RLVR is useless" but that the "pacing the frontier" discussion smuggles in a premise: it assumes everyone must do more RLVR, and RLVR looks dangerous because it lets the model "do anything they want" in the middle of training — the less you restrict it, the stronger the model is on the outside. So the danger is not a side effect, it is the design goal. He calls this a "disillusion of responsibility": taking "we must do more RLVR" as an axiom and then deriving the conclusion "we are heading toward a dangerous world."

2:09:13 The KV cache is a tyranny over coding agents
Diogo wants to explore coding agents "free from the tyranny of the KV cache." The KV cache locks you into one model, and for efficiency you have to keep appending, so you can't do state management, abstraction or decomposition — normal software practices. From this he explains several phenomena: why routing is hard, why sub-agents don't seem to work, why compaction is a hard problem — because passing state around requires intelligence that is much cheaper than reading state. The directions he imagines include: explicitly annotating state for subtasks, searching for relevant context in a tree of subtasks, parallel sub-agents reading each other's state, and coordinating with smart locks rather than basic-ass locks.

item.title: AI will hit an energy wall within three years, and the fix is to build a computer that isn't a computer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.description: Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.
item.content:encoded:
Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.

The first half is the energy math; the second half is his first public prototype of a physical dynamics computer and its measured efficiency numbers — rare hard information. The biology analogy in the middle can be fast-forwarded.

4:45 Energy isn't a cost line, it's the ticket to entry
Naveen's math: Google crosses 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, and at the low-end figure of 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts. The US today puts about 40 gigawatts into data centers; the world, under 100 gigawatts. So one company's AI service eats more than a tenth of global data center energy. His call is that we hit the energy ceiling in about three years. More to the point, the ranking of scarce resources in a data center has flipped: it used to be floor space, racks, networking gear, GPUs; today it's energy — get the power contract first, then figure out how to fill it. And energy is 50% of the cost of serving a token; only after that come hardware capex and the site.

7:04 What a squirrel does on 8 milliwatts, a GPU needs watts for
A human brain is about 20 watts. Scale linearly by neuron count down to a monkey brain and you get one watt — exactly your phone in your pocket. Further down, mice and bats are in the milliwatt range. A squirrel leaping between branches, a thousand times out of a thousand, does it on an 8-milliwatt brain. Which is to say your phone's battery could run a hundred-plus squirrel brains. Naveen's conclusion is that biology has already built a physical substrate suited to intelligence, and synthetic systems went another way: the human cortex moves only about 16 billion bits per second, while a high-end GPU moves close to 30 trillion bits per second in and out of memory, and inside the chip it's another 10 to 100 times higher. The energy goes almost entirely into moving information, not computing on it.

10:06 Moore's Law stopped; the abstraction layers still charge rent
Transistor counts are still climbing, but frequency stopped scaling long ago, single-thread performance stopped too, and now even efficiency no longer improves as process nodes shrink — Naveen says flatly that Moore's Law is basically over. His diagnosis is the abstraction layers: digital is itself an abstraction of the physical world, and transistors actually have intermediate states that get engineered into 0s and 1s. Every layer of abstraction is lossy and ignores the complexity beneath it. So their approach is to wire the physics of the semiconductor directly to the neural network and skip the layers in between. His intuition pump is flocks of birds and ant colonies: individuals doing extremely simple things, with complex behavior emerging at the whole — the field is called dynamical systems theory.

12:07 Metronomes on a board sync up on their own
Put several metronomes on a rigid board that can roll back and forth, and they will synchronize to exactly the same phase on their own, simply because each one gives the board a tiny push. That's a purely physical dynamical system. Their question was whether such a system can compute. The answer is yes — they open-sourced an image generation model called UNO built on a set of such oscillators, and it trains and produces images. Define the system state as the phases of all the oscillators, condition on the output, and generating a plane, a car or a bird follows a different state space trajectory. It's the first demonstration that this class of system can be trained at scale and produce useful results.

14:08 Throwing away connections makes the system easier to train
All-to-all is n squared: 10 elements and 100 connections is fine, 1000 elements is a million connections, and it doesn't scale at all. Their sparsity is deliberately discarding some fraction of connections and then seeing whether the overall behavior can be rescued. The result isn't just that you can throw them away — after discarding, the system behaves better and is more trainable, and that holds both in simulation and in real physical systems. Naveen calls this the rare case where more efficient, more scalable and better performing all hold at once, a holy grail nobody had cracked for a long time, provided you frame the problem correctly first.

15:09 The first physical dynamics computer has already generated images
This is Naveen's first public disclosure: they have built the first physical dynamics computer. The company only formally started in January of this year, with no team at the time; on June 1 they sent the design to tape-out, and the chip is already back in the lab with results — the first images generated by this kind of computer. On efficiency, generating an image takes about 500 nanojoules, versus millijoules for an ordinary GPU; a nanojoule is 10 to the minus 9, so that's several orders of magnitude. The reason is that it doesn't move information at all. Architecturally it's unlike both CPUs and GPUs: those are von Neumann architectures with memory and compute separated, shuttling data back and forth; in this machine compute and storage are the same thing, there is no memory interface, and every compute unit is itself a memory.

17:09 4D computing: three spatial dimensions plus one of time
They call the whole thing 4D computing: physically, die stacking uses all three dimensions vertically and in-plane, and the fourth dimension is time in the dynamics. The objective function is intelligence per watt. There is a thermodynamic limit that can never be crossed; animal brains are only one to two orders of magnitude away from it, while today's computing systems are about 10 billion times off. Their plan is to hit the limits of 2D lithography within three and a half years, and the company's overall goal is to beat biology. Naveen expects the result to be a change in form factor: from gigawatt-scale mega data centers toward small data centers scattered everywhere, more local, more adaptive, and supporting billions of robots that dynamically combine to solve problems.

19:12 A thousand times cheaper means a thousand times more consumption
Naveen closes with the Jevons paradox: when the underlying cost of an asset falls, consumption grows by more than the price fell. Halve the price and consumption more than doubles; cut the price to a thousandth and consumption grows more than a thousandfold. So he doesn't think efficiency gains shrink the market — they create the largest market in human history. Chamath then presses on the ecosystem — tape-out, packaging and so on need a whole set of people to coordinate. Naveen's answer is a complete product within two years, in the form of an entire rack, sold as a new data center product: tokens in, tokens out over the network, but internally structured completely differently from existing computers.

item.title: Strategic Reserves Are Nearly Drained — the Oil Price Crisis Is Only Now Beginning
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.description: Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only about to hit diesel and prices.
item.content:encoded:
Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only about to hit diesel and prices.

Medium information density, but breaking down "why oil didn't rise" into three buffers and the pace at which they're being exhausted is more useful than reading headlines.

2:03 Close Hormuz and a fifth of the world's oil is gone
The war began with Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, cutting off roughly 20% of global oil supply. This was the move everyone treated as the "nuclear option" — nobody wanted to see it, because it's too bad for all sides. Once the strait closed, oil shot from around $70 a barrel to well over $100. But the market didn't spiral out of control from there; it found several buffers that held prices down. The real question isn't "why did it rise" but "why didn't it rise more."

3:09 Three buffers, each less usable than the last
The first is the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve — emergency crude stored in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast after the 1970s Arab oil embargo — plus the commercial inventories refiners hold, both at high levels before the conflict. The second is sanctioned oil: a large volume of "dark fleet" crude from Iran and Russia drifting at sea, which in March the US temporarily allowed other countries to buy. The third is China — the world's largest oil importer, normally buying about 12 million barrels a day, roughly 10% of global supply, which earlier this year bought about 3 million barrels a day less, effectively giving that oil to others. Together these three held oil below $100 and the national average gasoline price just under $5.

6:12 Ceasefire talks made analysts look foolish en masse
In June the US and Iran began talks and reached a ceasefire, and market sentiment flipped 180 degrees: from "extreme crude shortage" to "crude surplus," with analysts predicting oil would fall to $70 or even $60 a barrel. But the peace deal collapsed within weeks, Iran closed the strait again, and Trump declared the ceasefire over. So it was back to the state at the start of the conflict. This episode shows one thing: this round of prices contains a lot of bets that "the war ends soon," and that bet has repeatedly failed.

8:15 Six months of draining, and the buffers are nearly dry
Commercial inventories have been drawn down, strategic reserves released — and reserves can't be released at will; the government authorized only a specific quantity. The US has taken more than 130 million barrels out of the strategic reserve, leaving about 280 million, which sounds like a lot but is approaching the authorized ceiling. Worse, this time there's an added refinery crisis: Middle Eastern refineries were struck in the war, and Ukraine, in self-defense, knocked out a large chunk of Russia's refining capacity — and Russia is the world's second-largest diesel exporter. Once a refinery is destroyed, it takes months to restore. So the problem now isn't whether there's crude; it's that there isn't enough refining capacity to produce the fuel the world needs.

9:16 Venezuela can't put out a fire this close
The Trump administration points to Venezuela as the solution, where reserves may be the world's largest. But reserves being there doesn't mean production capacity is there: to actually raise output you need to invest money, move rigs, hire people, drill, and ship the barrels out — roughly years of time and billions of dollars of investment. As for other "miracle solutions," Benoit says there basically aren't any; you can only hope for "small miracles" — like China deciding to raise diesel output, or refinery repairs finishing early. But none of these take effect tomorrow.

10:17 Gas stations haven't blown up yet — diesel blew up first
US consumers haven't yet seen prices spike at the pump; what's really rising is diesel — the fuel that drives the heavy trucks moving consumer goods from one end of the country to the other. The question therefore becomes: will companies cut back on deliveries? When do they pass costs on to consumers? Once diesel rises, every kind of business has to factor it into its pricing. This is the real channel through which this shock transmits from energy markets to the real economy, and why "gas prices are okay" is a misleading comfort.

12:23 Two paths: absorb it, or pass it on
Businesses have only two choices. One is to hold the line on prices: Jim Barber, a third-generation Pennsylvania farmer, has raised his beef price only once in five years, and even with the cost of hauling in hay up 15% to 20%, he eats it himself, because he values his relationship with customers and believes the conflict will end soon and that holding on will be rewarded. A farmer's fuel exposure is triple-layered — fertilizer, hauling in hay, and shipping his own goods out — so energy costs can be paid three times over or more. The second is to pass it on: Ambix, which makes plastic parts, uses resin, and resin comes from oil; some costs rose 30%, 40%, 50%. At first it resisted raising prices, but as the war dragged on it began passing the 60 cents its suppliers added straight to customers.

15:36 Six-dollar diesel in August, and the shock starts embedding in the economy
When energy prices eased this summer, many businesses had a spell of optimism, thinking maybe they were coming out of the woods. Then in August tensions heated up again, fuel prices rose again, and recently diesel hit $6 a gallon. Owen thinks this is the moment when some businesses and economists began to realize "the price shock is truly embedding in the economy." Meanwhile, JPMorgan commodity analysts said in their latest forecast that they no longer know how to model it — there's no baseline, because they can't see around the corner. On paper many economic indicators are healthy, but consumers feel terrible about prices, and nobody — oil executives, politicians, or CEOs — can say clearly how long this lasts.

item.title: Optimism Is Not a Personality Trait, It's an Explanatory Style You Can Train
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.description: Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.
item.content:encoded:
Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.

Seligman himself walks through the full chain from learned helplessness to learned optimism, and in the back half treats agency as a civilisational variable to be quantified — a rare angle.

9:36 The dog doesn't run, and it isn't because it never learned to run
In Solomon's lab, on day one the dog was strapped into a hammock and given Pavlovian shocks it could not escape no matter what it did; on day two it was put in a shuttle box where running to the other side would switch off the shock, and the dog just lay there. Seligman's reading: what the animal actually learned was not "the tone predicts a shock" but "nothing I do matters." That interpretation collided head-on with behaviourism at the time, because it required the animal to be a cognitive subject capable of thinking and of integrating experience across time.

13:50 People can be taught to give up by noise, too
